title: Leaked questions
topic: Probity in training, research, audit and applications
stem:
You are an F2 doctor revising for a postgraduate exam that you sit next month. In your year group's chat, a colleague posts a document that he says contains questions remembered by candidates from last week's sitting.

Candidates for this exam agree not to share its content. Several colleagues reply with thanks.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Download it but only use it to check your general knowledge.
options.brief: Still using content you shouldn't have.
options.detailed: However you use it, you would be benefiting from material shared in breach of the exam's rules.

options.text: Forward it to friends sitting the exam at another trust.
options.detailed: This makes the problem worse and involves you directly in sharing it.

options.text: Don't open or use the document.
options.brief: Using leaked exam content would be dishonest.
options.detailed: Candidates agree not to share exam content. Using it to prepare would give you an unfair advantage and break the conditions of the exam.

options.text: Reply in the group chat condemning the post.
options.brief: Publicly shaming him isn't the most effective approach.
options.detailed: Your concern is valid, but a public rebuke may cause conflict without getting the document removed. A private word is better first.

options.text: Message him privately, asking him to delete it.
options.brief: A direct, private word gives him the chance to put it right.
options.detailed: He may not have thought about the consequences. A private message explaining that sharing exam content breaches the exam's rules, and asking him to remove it, is fair and may stop it spreading.

options.text: Ask your educational supervisor whether to report it.
options.brief: Helps you decide whether it needs to go further.
options.detailed: Sharing exam content may need reporting to the exam body. Your supervisor can help you judge this, particularly if the document isn't removed.

options.text: Report it to the royal college that runs the exam, naming your colleague.
options.brief: The exam body may need to know, but reporting him by name first skips simpler steps.
options.detailed: Breaches of exam rules can be reported to the body that runs the exam, and that may become appropriate. Doing it first, naming him, without speaking to him or taking advice, is heavy-handed when he may simply delete it.

options.text: Leave the group chat so you aren't involved.
options.brief: Protects you, but does nothing about the problem.
options.detailed: Leaving avoids the issue rather than dealing with it, and others may still use the material.

explanation.issue: This tests honesty in assessment and how you respond when colleagues share material they shouldn't.
explanation.keyDetails: The document contains questions remembered from the exam. Candidates agree not to share them. Others are already using it.
explanation.reasoning: [C] keeps your own preparation honest, [E] addresses it with your colleague, and [F] gets advice on reporting it. The distractors use it ([A]), spread it ([B]), shame him publicly ([D]), escalate disproportionately ([G]), or avoid it ([H]).
explanation.competing: [D] is tempting because it is quick and principled. A private message is more likely to get the document removed without conflict.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 4, honesty in examinations and assessments.
